settings.paragraph: Behavioral health billing at the program level brings together three things outpatient billing rarely handles at once: per diem claims, authorizations that renew every few days and federal privacy rules for substance use records. When one review is missed or one code doesn’t match, a full week of treatment can go unpaid. Here are six places where program revenue commonly slips through.

styles.css: color: var(--DarkGray); line-height: 24px; text-align: center;

settings.paragraph: Payers usually approve residential, PHP and IOP stays a few days at a time. Each extension needs a concurrent review with current clinical notes before the last covered day. A step-down to a lower level of care needs its own authorization too. If either one is missed, the days your team already treated can go unpaid.

Medicare certifies PHP patients for at least 20 hours of treatment a week and IOP patients for 9 to 19 hours. Payment is made per day. A PHP day needs at least three qualifying services, while IOP pays a higher rate for days with four or more. Commercial and Medicaid plans set their own minimums. Days without enough documented services, or without start and stop times, may be denied or underpaid.

Program services are billed on the UB-04 with a bill type, revenue codes and, for Medicare, a condition code: 92 for IOP and 41 for PHP. Services from psychiatrists and nurse practitioners go on the CMS-1500. A single mismatch between the revenue code, HCPCS code and condition code can get the entire claim rejected.

A patient’s insurance card doesn’t always show who pays the behavioral health claim. Many plans hand behavioral benefits to a separate company, so the card names one insurer while the claims belong to another. Out-of-network programs often need a single case agreement before admission. Without one, payment depends on out-of-network benefits or falls to the patient.

Some plans cap visits, require stricter prior authorization or ask for more frequent reviews for behavioral care than for comparable medical care. The Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act restricts limits like these. We flag them, raise parity in appeals and, with the patient’s authorization, request the plan’s comparative analysis.

Substance use disorder programs covered by 42 CFR Part 2 need written patient consent before records go to a payer. Its latest 2024 update permits a single consent for treatment, payment and health care operations. And compliance has been required since February 16, 2026. Every claim, appeal and records request needs to stay within the consent on file.

settings.title: Behavioral Health Billing Services by Level of Care

settings.paragraph: Each level of care comes with its own claim forms, revenue codes, authorization cycle and denial pattern, and the rules shift again from one payer to the next. Here’s how our behavioral health billing services handle each one.

IOPs operate in hospital outpatient departments, community mental health centers and freestanding programs. Since January 1, 2024, Medicare has also covered IOP in FQHCs, RHCs and opioid treatment programs. Medicare IOP billing uses the UB-04 (bill type 13X or 76X) with condition code 92, and each service goes on its own lines with a revenue code and a CPT or HCPCS code. Commercial plans generally pay a per diem, and IOP billing codes depend on the contract: S9480 under revenue code 0905 for psychiatric IOP or H0015 under 0906 for SUD IOP. Authorizations are usually approved a few days at a time.

Hospitals and CMHCs run PHPs for patients who need at least 20 hours of treatment a week. Medicare partial hospitalization billing uses the UB-04 with condition code 41 and the same line-by-line revenue codes as IOP. Medicare pays one per diem for each day with three or more services. A physician must certify that the patient needs this level of care and recertify it periodically. Commercial and Medicaid plans often pay a per diem billed with S0201 or H0035 under revenue code 0912 or 0913, with frequent reviews.

Licensed residential programs provide round-the-clock mental health and substance use treatment outside a hospital. Residential treatment billing uses the UB-04 with revenue code 1001 (psychiatric) or 1002 (chemical dependency), usually as a per diem. Medicaid plans often require H0018 (short-term) or H0019 (long-term), which exclude room and board. Medicare doesn’t cover non-hospital residential treatment. For adults in facilities with more than 16 beds, Medicaid’s IMD exclusion limits payment unless the state has a Section 1115 waiver. Reviews typically come every few days.

Withdrawal management ranges from ambulatory detox to medically managed inpatient care, depending on the patient’s ASAM level. Non-hospital residential detox is billed per diem with H0010 (sub-acute) or H0011 (acute), on the UB-04 or CMS-1500, depending on the payer. Hospital-based detox is billed as an inpatient stay with detox room-and-board revenue codes such as 0116 or 0126. Since approvals are short and reviewed often, our rehab billing services confirm benefits and authorization at admission.

settings.title: Community Mental Health Centers and CCBHCs

settings.paragraph: CMHCs bill Medicare for PHP and IOP on bill type 76X, following the same condition code and line-item rules as hospitals. CCBHCs are paid by state Medicaid programs through a prospective payment system: a daily rate (PPS-1), a monthly rate (PPS-2) or either one with separate crisis service rates (PPS-3 and PPS-4). In community behavioral health billing, the qualifying visit is what triggers the payment, so CCBHC billing depends on capturing every qualifying visit.

settings.title: Outpatient Therapy, Psychiatry and Psychological Testing

settings.paragraph: Many programs also offer outpatient services, which are billed on the CMS-1500. Psychotherapy uses time-based codes (90832, 90834, 90837). Psychiatrists and nurse practitioners pair E/M visits with psychotherapy add-ons (90833, 90836, 90838), while psychological testing uses 96130-96139. If your practice offers only outpatient care, see our mental health billing services, psychiatric billing services and psychology billing services.

Applied behavior analysis is billed on the CMS-1500 in 15-minute units under 97151-97158, and payers authorize a set number of units per week or month. Each code has its own rules on who can deliver it, and payers set supervision requirements for RBTs working under a BCBA. Our ABA billing services track units against each authorization, so your team doesn’t deliver sessions beyond what was approved.

settings.title: Collaborative Care and Behavioral Health Integration

settings.paragraph: When medical groups add behavioral health, they bill the psychiatric Collaborative Care Model monthly with 99492, 99493 and 99494, and general behavioral health integration with 99484. These time-based codes are billed by the treating practitioner with patient consent on file and minutes tracked across the month. FQHCs and RHCs follow different rules. For those, see our FQHC billing services.

settings.title: Coding and Charge Capture by Level of Care

settings.paragraph: Your claims should reflect the services documented. Our coders review per diem billing, revenue codes and applicable CPT and HCPCS codes against the payer’s requirements. We check service counts, required start and stop times, and treatment plans, requesting clarification when supporting information is missing.

We prepare facility claims on the UB-04 (837I) and professional claims on the CMS-1500 (837P), following the applicable billing requirements. Our team reviews bill types, condition codes and payer edits before submission. These checks help identify errors while your practice can still address them.

When a claim is denied, your team needs to know why and what to do next. We review the denial, correct submission errors and prepare appropriate appeals with supporting documentation. If coverage restrictions raise potential mental health parity concerns, we address those issues in the appeal.

Our A/R team works every open claim by age and payer, including out-of-network and single case agreement claims, which usually need more follow-up. We escalate aging accounts before they reach the payer's timely filing limit.

We post payments from ERAs and EOBs, then compare each one with your contracted or agreed rate. Underpaid per diems and short-paid single case agreements are flagged and appealed rather than written off.

At admission, we explain each patient's expected costs, provide Good Faith Estimates to self-pay patients and send clear statements afterward. Setting up payment plans early helps keep patient balances from turning into bad debt.

settings.paragraph: Behavioral health programs answer to more rules than most practices do. These include federal privacy law for addiction records, parity law, Medicare’s IOP and PHP conditions and CMS behavioral health billing guidelines for telehealth. We build each one into the billing workflow, so your claims are prepared to hold up in an audit.

settings.title: 42 CFR Part 2 and SUD Record Confidentiality

settings.paragraph: 42 CFR Part 2 protects records from federally assisted substance use disorder programs more strictly than HIPAA alone. The 2024 final rule brought Part 2 closer to HIPAA by allowing one patient consent to cover treatment, payment and health care operations. Compliance has been required since February 16, 2026, and violations now carry HIPAA-level penalties. We release records only within the consent on file.

When a payer limits behavioral health coverage, your team needs to understand whether those restrictions meet parity requirements. MHPAEA generally prevents applicable plans from imposing more restrictive financial requirements or treatment limitations than permitted for comparable medical care. Federal agencies have paused enforcement of provisions newly introduced by the 2024 rule, but existing statutory obligations remain. We review potential concerns and identify issues that may support an appeal.

settings.paragraph: Your records need to support the physician’s certification and the patient’s treatment needs. Medicare requires at least 20 hours weekly for PHP and at least nine for IOP. Applicable facility claims use condition code 41 for PHP or 92 for IOP, with services reported by date. We check required time records and certification schedules, including IOP recertification at least every 60 days, before submission.

Medicare permanently covers behavioral health telehealth in the patient's home. Its in-person visit requirement for tele-mental health has been delayed to January 1, 2028, and audio-only coverage runs through December 31, 2027. Each claim needs the right place of service (02 or 10) and modifier (95 for video, 93 for audio-only). Commercial and Medicaid rules vary by plan.

settings.title: No Surprises Act for Self-Pay Clients

settings.paragraph: Your uninsured and self-pay patients generally need a written Good Faith Estimate when care is requested or scheduled within applicable timelines. A bill at least $400 above that provider’s estimate may qualify for dispute. We help prepare estimates around the planned services and expected length of stay.

MedCare MSO works as a HIPAA-compliant business associate. We sign a business associate agreement, limit access to patient records by role and use only the minimum information needed to bill each claim.
Behavioral health insurance billing involves more payer types than a typical medical practice deals with, and often two companies for the same patient. Our team bills:
Hospital and CMHC IOP and PHP, plus professional services from psychiatrists, psychologists, LCSWs, marriage and family therapists and mental health counselors.
State-specific H-codes, modifiers and authorization rules, including CCBHC PPS billing.
Per diem contracts for IOP, PHP, residential and detox.
Optum Behavioral Health, Carelon Behavioral Health, Magellan Health and Evernorth Behavioral Health.
Claims following the program’s referral, authorization and submission requirements.
Approved sessions billed using the EAP’s authorization details.
Out-of-network care billed according to negotiated payment terms.

Coverage can differ sharply by level of care. For example, Medicare doesn’t pay for non-hospital residential treatment, so residential programs rely on commercial plans, self-pay and Medicaid where state waivers allow it.

settings.paragraph: How much do behavioral health billing services cost?

The service charges depend on various factors. They include the levels of care you provide, claim volume, payer mix and the required support. Most programs pay a percentage of collections, with no setup fees. You can choose full revenue cycle management or assistance with specific tasks, such as A/R recovery or credentialing. Our free audit helps us review your billing needs and prepare a customized quote.
How do you bill IOP and PHP services?

We check your program’s settings and payer requirements before preparing claims. Medicare hospital and CMHC claims use the UB-04 with condition code 92 for IOP or 41 for PHP and individual service lines. Commercial and Medicaid contracts may require per diem codes such as S9480, H0015, S0201 or H0035. We review applicable authorizations, service counts and required time documentation before submission.
Are behavioral health programs billed on a UB-04 or a CMS-1500?

Your program may need both forms, depending on the services and payer. Facility claims generally use the UB-04 (837I), while separately billable professional services use the CMS-1500 (837P). Some Medicaid programs and commercial contracts require freestanding programs to submit per diem claims on the CMS-1500. We check the applicable requirements before deciding how each service should be billed.
How do you handle concurrent reviews and authorization renewals?

Your team needs to know when approved coverage ends and what the payer requires next. We record authorization dates, schedule reviews and coordinate with your clinical staff for updated notes, treatment plans and discharge progress. If a patient moves to a lower level of care, we request any required authorization before that treatment begins and follow up on the payer’s decision.
How do you protect SUD records under 42 CFR Part 2?

Before sharing protected SUD records for billing, we check the patient’s consent and applicable disclosure requirements. The updated Part 2 rule, with compliance required since February 16, 2026, permits one consent for treatment, payment and healthcare operations. Our team examines consent before sending claims, appeals or supporting records, with staff access assigned according to their responsibilities.
Can you bill out-of-network payers and single case agreements?

Yes. We review relevant benefits before admission and request a single case agreement where appropriate. If the payer approves an agreement, we bill according to its terms, track outstanding claims and follow up on payment differences. We support Good Faith Estimates under the applicable No Surprises Act requirements for uninsured or self-pay patients.
What is the difference between behavioral health billing and mental health billing?

The terms overlap. Mental health billing usually refers to outpatient services billed on the CMS-1500: therapy sessions, psychiatric visits and testing. Behavioral health billing is broader. It also covers substance use treatment and program-level care such as IOP, PHP, residential and detox, which are billed per diem on the UB-04 with their own authorizations. If you run an outpatient practice, see our mental health billing services.
How long does it take to switch behavioral health billing companies?

Most programs move over in 4 to 8 weeks. The timeline depends on how many levels of care and payers you have, and whether credentialing or EHR access needs updating. During the parallel run, your current process continues until we confirm every open authorization and claim is covered, so nothing stalls during the switch.
